title: How Artico works
goal: A little understanding. A lot of meaningful practice.

study.title: Begin where it helps you.
paragraphs: Some learners are meeting the alphabet for the first time. Others know grammar well but find ordinary speech difficult to follow. Some already communicate and want more control over their pronunciation.
Artico starts with the basics, but Foundations is open to explore, repeat, or skip. There is no placement test or penalty for changing your mind.
If the letters and basic sounds are familiar, take a quick look. You might notice something useful. Otherwise, go straight to the conversations and return when a foundation lesson would help.

study.title: One learning path. Two modes.
paragraphs: Orientation introduces the big picture. Foundations explores letters, sounds, mouth movements, and rhythm. Social Fluency brings those skills into everyday situations.
Inside a lesson, Study explains what is happening and why the language fits. Practice gives you space to say, recall, adapt, and repeat it.
These are places you can move between. You can work on a sound while learning a conversation and return to an explanation whenever you need it.
items: Orientation — your reason and your route.
Social Fluency — words for everyday interaction.
Study — understand the context and examples.
Practice — choose useful phrases, say them, and try a situation.

study.title: Get comfortable with the sounds.
paragraphs: English has 26 letters, but letters and speech sounds are different things. The number of sounds depends on the accent and the analysis used; a familiar teaching chart is a guide, not a universal count.
A letter can represent different sounds. Different spellings can represent the same sound. Knowing a written word does not guarantee that you will recognize it in connected speech.
Tongue twisters isolate a difficult movement so you can repeat it without also inventing a sentence. They are useful practice tools, but they do not teach conversation by themselves.
Work on sound contrasts, consonant clusters, word endings, vowels, airflow, stress, and rhythm. Notice the target, start with a clear short chunk, then bring the movement into an ordinary phrase.
Keep returning to these movements as you study conversations. A short routine can support regular practice; no fixed number of weeks guarantees perfect pronunciation.
note: If the sounds start to blur, slow down or shorten the phrase. Practice a movement you can control.

study.title: Bring it into a conversation.
paragraphs: Begin Social Fluency whenever you feel ready. You do not need to finish every sound exercise first.
The chapters begin with greetings, short responses, questions, invitations, reactions, feelings, and small stories. They then widen the range of situations and relationships.
The examples focus on language that helps people do something together: respond, clarify, arrange, disagree, explain, and keep a conversation going.
A café, workplace, station, shop, hobby group, or video call is a starting context. The pattern can travel with you into other parts of your life.

study.title: A simple lesson rhythm.
paragraphs: Start with the scene and its meaning. Notice a useful phrase. Practice it with support, then try to recall and adapt it. Return after a little time has passed.
items: See the situation: who is speaking, and what do they need?
Read the explanation and connect it to the examples.
Listen to a model when audio is available.
Notice the wording, rhythm, and choice of response.
Choose phrases and rehearse them aloud.
Hide the phrase, recall it, and change a detail.
Try a small use outside the lesson.
Come back later and try it again.

study.title: Study helps the language make sense.
paragraphs: An explanation is there to make a phrase understandable. You do not need to memorize every paragraph.
First, see the interaction as a whole. Then look at the details: why a phrase fits, how direct it sounds, and what changes with tone or relationship. Finally, return to the scene.

A useful check is whether you can explain the idea simply in your own words. Illustrations support context, phrase cards separate the words you can say, and diagrams make certain relationships easier to see.

study.title: Give yourself time to say it.
paragraphs: Recognizing an explanation and finding words while someone waits are different experiences. Practice connects them through speaking, remembering, changing a detail, and trying again.
The phrase list contains the words and examples from Study. Tick the ones you want, and leave others for later. A selection is not a score or a claim that you have learned something.

Your selected set stays together for the round. Hide and reveal a phrase, save it, or mark how familiar it feels. These are your own assessments. When the phrases feel easier, try the situations and compare a sample response.
items: Listen first when a recording is available.
Notice one feature and say the phrase clearly.
Repeat it a few times with attention.
Use less text support and recall it.
Change a detail or answer as another person.
Return later and check how it feels.

study.title: Listening and rehearsal have different needs.
paragraphs: Natural listening models show the context, feeling, rhythm, and turn-taking of an everyday conversation. Rehearsal recordings can add clear chunks and useful space to repeat.
The aim is natural language that you can gradually follow and use. A rehearsal track is more than a recording slowed down without attention to its rhythm.

Chapter recordings are still being prepared. Their controls say when audio is unavailable. Some Foundation examples already have audio or linked videos; alphabet buttons use your device’s speech voice.

study.title: A complete lesson, an open world.
paragraphs: The lesson keeps its explanations, written models, illustrations, practice prompts, and sample responses together so you can work without assembling your own materials.
That does not mean the course covers all of English. Dictionaries, people, films, travel, and unexpected phrases will always show you more. Bring those discoveries back to what you are learning.

study.title: Take one small step beyond the screen.
paragraphs: Try a greeting, ask a colleague a short question, or use a clarification phrase when you need one. Choose an action that fits the situation and the other person.
You can also practice alone: leave yourself a voice note, adapt a phrase to your own life, notice it in a video, or rehearse before a call.
Artico cannot verify every conversation you have. It can help you choose a small, clear, relevant next step.

study.title: Keep your voice.
paragraphs: Being understood is a useful first goal. You may later choose a particular speaker’s rhythm, precision, or energy as a model.
This course uses General American English as its main reference. That does not make other accents incorrect, and it does not mean you need to become a different person.
Aim for clear, dependable speech and attention to the people you are talking with. Develop your own preferences as you gain experience.

study.title: Make a small start today.
paragraphs: Read Orientation, glance through Foundations, and choose a starting point that is useful now. This edition’s guidance is in English.
Study one conversation. Pick a small set of phrases to say aloud. Try a sound exercise alongside it if that helps. Spend some of your time actually speaking, rather than only rereading explanations.

Your place, notes, saved phrases, and selections stay on this device. Device sync and scheduled review reminders are not available yet. Progress shows what you opened and the ratings you gave yourself.

study.title: A clear path, without a deadline for fluency.
paragraphs: Artico does not promise fluency in 30 or 90 days. Moving quickly through screens is not the same thing as learning to communicate.
The aim is a coherent path, useful explanations, meaningful models, and clear practice you can return to.
The app can organize the next step. You bring it to life by paying attention and trying it.

study.title: Start with the letters.
paragraphs: Next, meet the 26 letters. Then separate letter names from speech sounds, notice how sounds are made, and begin a pronunciation routine.
Some of it may be familiar. You can check the foundations without proving that you are a beginner, and move on when you are ready.
